The sexton stood in the porch of the Milford meeting house, pulling busily at the bell rope, while the old people of the village came stooping along the street. <break time="0.8s" /> But what has good Parson Hooper got upon his face, cried the sexton in astonishment, as the minister came slowly along the street toward the meeting house. <break time="0.8s" /> Mister Hooper, a gentlemanly man of about thirty who was still a bachelor, was dressed neatly, but there was one thing remarkable in his appearance. <break time="0.8s" /> Swathed about his forehead and hanging down over his face was a black veil, which entirely concealed his features except the mouth and chin. <break time="0.8s" /> Our parson has gone mad, cried Goodman Gray, and a strange murmur spread through the meeting house as the veiled minister walked slowly up the aisle. <break time="0.8s" /> Many people turned around in their seats to stare, and several little boys climbed upon the benches and came down again with a terrible racket. <break time="0.8s" /> That day he preached about secret sin, about the sad mysteries which we hide from our nearest and dearest, and even from our own consciousness. <break time="0.8s" /> Each member of the congregation, even the most innocent girl, felt as if the preacher had crept upon them behind his awful veil and discovered their hidden sins.

After the service, the people hurried out of the meeting house, some gathering in little circles to whisper and others walking home alone, wrapped in silent thought. <break time="0.8s" /> Old Squire Saunders, doubtless by an accidental lapse of memory, neglected to invite Mister Hooper to his table, where the good minister had blessed the food almost every Sunday. <break time="0.8s" /> How strange, said the doctors wife, that a simple black veil, such as any woman might wear on her bonnet, should become so terrible on Mister Hoopers face. <break time="0.8s" /> That afternoon Mister Hooper attended the funeral of a young lady, and as he bent over the coffin, his veil hung straight down from his forehead. <break time="0.8s" /> Had her eyelids not been closed forever, the dead maiden might have seen his face, and he hastily caught back the veil as if fearing her glance. <break time="0.8s" /> A superstitious old woman, the only witness of this wonder, declared that at the instant when the ministers features were disclosed, the corpse had slightly shuddered. <break time="0.8s" /> That night, at the wedding of the handsomest couple in Milford, his veil cast such a gloom over the party that the joyful evening seemed like a funeral. <break time="0.8s" /> When he raised a glass of wine and caught sight of his own figure in the mirror, he shuddered, spilled the wine, and rushed out into the darkness.
